title: Arizona voter law fight reaches SCOTUS as election groups warn ‘absurd’ consequence could ensue
summary: Election experts warn the Supreme Court that the 9th Circuit's ruling could make it impossible to ever remove noncitizens from state voter rolls.
story: Federal prosecutors charged a Honduran national with voter fraud in California after he allegedly registered to vote under an alias and cast ballots in multiple elections. Fox News' Matt Finn reports on the federal indictment details, revealing the suspect received a voter registration card using a gym membership.

Election experts are warning the Supreme Court that affirming a lower court's ruling could mean that noncitizens, minors or factitious people listed on state voter rolls could be impossible to remove.

The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in RNC v. Mi Familia Vote in December and will determine whether a pair of Arizona's state laws that remove the registrations of noncitizen voters from voter rolls within 90 days of an election and require voters to show proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote are in violation of the National Voter Registration Act.

"Citizenship is a qualification for voting. If states are going to enforce that requirement, they have to be able to verify it," Justin Riemer, president and CEO of Restoring Integrity and Trust in Elections said in a statement to Fox News Digital.
CLINTON-APPOINTED JUDGE TRIGGERS APPEAL AFTER BLOCKING KEY VOTER CITIZENSHIP LAW

"And when officials find noncitizens on the voter rolls, they should be able to act before an election, not after. We are confident the Supreme Court will agree and reverse the Ninth Circuit's misguided ruling."

In an amicus brief filed Thursday, attorneys from Center for Election Confidence, Inc.; Restoring Integrity and Trust in Elections, Inc.; and Honest Elections Project, argued the 9th Circuit Court's ruling that the Arizona laws are an act of "voter suppression" is "absurd" and raises serious threats to state rights.

Voters arrive at a polling location at the Burton Barr Central Library Nov. 5, 2024, in Phoenix, Ariz. RNC v. Mi Familia Vote will determine whether a pair of Arizona's state laws that remove the registrations of noncitizen voters from voter rolls within 90 days of the election and require voters to show proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote violate the National Voter Registration Act. (Christian Petersen/Getty Images)

The brief argued that Congress may regulate the mechanics of federal elections, but states have the constitutional authority to set and enforce voter qualifications, a power they argued becomes meaningless if states cannot obtain documentation needed to verify citizenship or remove people who were never eligible to register.

"Since the power to establish voting requirements is of little value without the power to enforce those requirements, it would raise serious constitutional doubts if a federal statute precluded a State from obtaining the information necessary to enforce its voter qualifications," the brief stated.

The amicus brief pushed back on the 9th Circuit’s conclusion that Arizona cannot conduct a systematic program to remove noncitizens from voter rolls during the NVRA’s 90-day pre-election period. The federal law generally requires states to complete systematic voter-removal programs at least 90 days before a federal election, while allowing removals during that window for a voter’s request, death, criminal conviction or mental incapacity.
DEMOCRAT NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR SAYS THOUSANDS OF NONCITIZENS DISCOVERED ON VOTER ROLLS, PURGED

A volunteer picks up a "Require Voter ID" sign at the nes conference at the Riverside County Registrar of Voters March 2, 2026, as GOP lawmakers gather in support of placing a voter ID measure on the November ballot. (Anjali Sharif-Paul/MediaNews Group/The Sun via Getty Images)

The groups argued that noncitizenship is not among those listed grounds because it concerns someone who was never eligible to register in the first place. They said the restriction is meant to protect eligible voters from erroneous last-minute removals, not to shield people who were never eligible to register.

"If the Ninth Circuit is right that the 90-day limitation on programs prohibits removal on these bases — because the statute has listed exceptions — States could never remove improperly registered individuals who fall within these categories, no matter when the removal happens or whether it is after a systematic inquiry," the brief said.
"Not just that, but these States could never remove these noncitizens who were never eligible to vote."

The brief pointed to reported registration errors in New Jersey, Illinois and Oregon as examples of why states need a mechanism to correct allegedly improper registrations. It argues that an unlawful ballot cannot be undone once cast and counted.
DHS APPROVES PLAN TO VERIFY VOTER CITIZENSHIP, MONITOR MAIL BALLOTS AS TRUMP PUSH INTENSIFIES

"American elections are for American citizens only. Period," Lisa Dixon, executive director of the Center for Election Confidence, said in a statement. "We should all support Arizona ensuring noncitizens can’t register to vote and removing any non-citizens who end up on the voter lists."

The amici also argued that the 9th Circuit misread NVRA provisions governing what information is "necessary" for state election officials to assess a voter’s eligibility, and whether a state registration form is "equivalent" to the federal form.
Security guards stand in front of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco, Calif., June 12, 2017.  (Getty Images)

The brief argued that the 9th Circuit wrongly concluded a voter’s citizenship attestation on a registration form is sufficient proof of eligibility and improperly interpreted an "equivalent" state form to mean one that is virtually identical to the federal form.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Once again, far-left activists are using the courts to twist federal law into a straitjacket that prevents states from securing their elections," Jason Snead, executive director of Honest Elections Project, said in a statement to Fox News.
"The Honest Elections Project urges the Supreme Court to side with Arizona and preserve the tools states need to ensure that elections are decided only by American citizens."
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Well-connected Dem operative learns fate after FBI busts him in child sex abuse sting
summary: A former Virginia Democratic Party finance chair and 2024 DNC delegate was sentenced to a decade behind bars for child sexual abuse material and other child sex abuse allegations.
story: Democratic consultant Julian Epstein and former RNC general counsel Alex Vogel join 'Fox News Live' to analyze Democratic candidates rejecting campaign appearances from Joe Biden and Kamala Harris after new polling data was revealed.

A well-connected political consultant in Virginia with ties to the state's Democratic Party was sentenced to 10 years in federal prison after getting caught with child sexual abuse material and attempting to sexually abuse an undercover agent's purported 9-year-old son in an undercover FBI child sex abuse sting.

Randon Sprinkle, 31, of Richmond, was sentenced to 10 years in prison Thursday by U.S. District Judge Roderick C. Young after a federal investigation by the FBI’s Child Exploitation and Human Trafficking Task Force, according to a Justice Department press release.

According to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Virginia, Sprinkle was ensnared in a May 2025 undercover operation after making contact on a dating app called Jack'd with an agent posing as the father of a 9-year-old boy.

Authorities said Sprinkle sent the undercover agent a video showing two adults sexually abusing a minor; voiced a desire to travel to Washington, D.C., to abuse the fictitious child; and was later found in possession of dozens of files depicting the sexual abuse of toddlers and infants when agents searched his home.
FBI RAIDS SPANBERGER ALLY OFFICE AS FEDERAL CORRUPTION PROBE TARGETS CANNABIS BUSINESS
Virginia Democratic operative Randon Sprinkle was sentenced to 10 years in federal prison for child sexual abuse charges. (Getty Images)

In addition to serving as the finance chairman for the Democratic Party of Virginia and the treasurer for the Metro Richmond Area Young Democrats, Sprinkle served as an elected delegate to the 2024 Democratic National Convention, according to public party rosters and local reporting. He also worked as a paid political director for Rep. Jennifer McClellan’s 2021 gubernatorial bid and previously served as her legislative aide when she was a state senator.
Sprinkle has also worked for other Virginia Democratic Party campaigns, according to consulting payments, including state Sen. Jennifer Boysko.
The Virginia Capitol in Richmond, Va. (AP Photo/Steve Helber, File)

State campaign finance records compiled by the Virginia Public Access Project (VPAP) also show Sprinkle, who worked as an associate for the Richmond-based Reflex Strategy Group and another consulting group called Alexander Strategies LLC, donated thousands of dollars to the recent statewide campaigns of Rep. Abigail Spanberger and Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi.

Alleged photos preserved online after his arrest show Sprinkle regularly operating alongside national-level Democratic Party politicians as well, including former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, whose name has been floated for a presidential run in 2028; Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer; and Spanberger, among others.
Spanberger's transition team previously released a statement after his arrest, thanking the FBI "for their investigative work and for bringing this predator to justice."

"As a former federal law enforcement officer who arrested child predators, she believes that this individual should be swiftly prosecuted and put behind bars for his sickening crimes against children," the statement said.

"Upon learning about these appalling reports, the Spanberger campaign immediately donated the full amount of this individual’s prior donations, $1,000, to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children to support its critical mission of protecting America’s kids."
ILLEGAL ALIEN'S ‘INEXCUSABLE’ CRIME SPARKS INTERSTATE CLASH BETWEEN GOP SEN, DEM GOV: ‘YOU SHOULD BE ASHAMED’

When reached for comment, the Metro Richmond Area Young Democrats referred Fox News Digital to a statement issued by the organization’s executive board after Sprinkle's initial indictment in December 2025, confirming they took "immediate action to terminate all ties."

"The alleged conduct outlined in the indictment is reprehensible, unforgivable, and fundamentally misaligned with the values of our organization," the board said in the statement. "It violates the most basic standards of humanity and decency."
Randon Sprinkle was arrested after being busted in an undercover FBI child sex abuse sting. (iStock)

Fox News Digital also reached out to the Democratic Party of Virginia and the public defender representing Sprinkle but did not hear back in time for publication.

title: Ex-Fetterman staffers promise more damaging details after blistering report: ‘Tip of the iceberg’
summary: Former staff members for John Fetterman launched an X account promising damaging revelations well beyond The Wall Street Journal report.
story: Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., issued a fiery rebuttal to former Maine Democratic Senate candidate Graham Platner after he dropped out of the race after sexual assault allegations on ‘Jesse Watters Primetime.’
In just over a week, former staffers for John Fetterman, D-Pa., are planning to go public with inside details after expressing what they called disgust at his work as a legislator.

"We’re a group of former campaign & Senate staffers for John Fetterman who are disgusted with what he's become. If you were troubled by yesterday's Wall Street Journal story... trust us, that's just the tip of the iceberg," the group wrote in a post to X.
"It’s even worse than you thought."

The new social media account, which is calling itself "Former Fetterman Staffers" (FFS) claims it will reveal additional unflattering details about the embattled senator’s office as he also faces blowback over Wall Street Journal reporting chronicling his reluctance to engage in the basic duties of his office.
FETTERMAN FACES DEM REVOLT AS BOMBSHELL REPORT FUELS PUSH TO OUST HIM: 'DISGRACE'
Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., speaks to members of the media after a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., July 22, 2025. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The FFS acronym notoriously also stands for "for f---s sake."

Fetterman routinely blew off constituent meetings, neglected legislative review and declined to make in-state public appearances, according to a Wall Street Journal report published Thursday, drawing immediate backlash online.

"There is a lot I could say about this report of John Fetterman’s pathetic behavior as a senator," Rep. Chris Deluzio, D-Pa., said on X. "But between the laziness, disrespect, and willingness to carry water for a foreign government, it shows us something we already know: this man has no sense of duty."
"John Fetterman is a disgrace," Rep. Brendan Boyle, D-Pa., said in a post of his own. "Our state deserves better than a lazy trust fund baby who is too lazy to do the job."
Pennsylvania state Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta, who is the vice chair of the Democratic National Committee, also condemned Fetterman’s behavior.
"This report is horrifying, but not new to many of us in PA. John barely showed up as [Lieutenant Governor] and is constantly MIA as our senator," Kenyatta wrote.
"When he’s not on FOX cheerleading Trump & endless wars, he is attacking the very neighbors who gave him a chance. 2028 can’t come soon enough."
DNC VICE CHAIR ATTACKS DEMOCRATIC SEN. JOHN FETTERMAN: 'YOU’RE A MESS'

Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., speaks to reporters after a briefing by Trump administration officials to members of the Senate on U.S. strikes on Iran at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., March 3, 2026 (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Conor Lamb, a former Pennsylvania congressman who ran against Fetterman in the 2022 primary for the party’s nomination, called on Fetterman to resign.

"John, if there is a decent bone left in your body, just quit. It’s an insult to decent people in our state for you to treat them and the office this way," Lamb wrote, referring to an instance where Fetterman blew off a meeting with paralyzed military veterans.
As reactions continue to pour in, Former Fetterman Staffers, the new group on X, told viewers that they would set a deadline for some of its upcoming revelations.
"Set your calendar for September 14th — the day the Senate is back in session — for our first drop. (Let's be honest, maybe the 15th: he'll skip Monday's votes)," the group said.
Despite raising questions and rage toward Fetterman, some observers condemned the staffers for what they called a lack of loyalty.

"So disloyal. He gave you jobs and opportunities and advanced your careers, and you publicly turn on him and set up an X account to attack him?" Marc Thiessen, a political pundit and former White House speechwriter for the Bush administration, wrote on X.
"Honorable thing, if you disagree, is to resign quietly and work for someone else you prefer. You are pathetic."
Mark Morgan, political director for the Republican Governors Association, echoed Thiessen's thinking, blasting the group for its anonymity.

"Staff rule #1: it's not about you Staff rule #2: Your boss had the courage to put their name on a ballot. If you've chosen to become a click-seeking bottom feeder, at least have the courage to put your own name on it," Morgan said.
EMBATTLED REP TONY GONZALES ANNOUNCES PLANS TO RESIGN AMID SEXUAL MISCONDUCT ALLEGATIONS
U.S. Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., speaks to reporters outside the Senate Chamber during votes on Nov. 10, 2025, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
"I’m disgusted by anonymous leakers, actually," Harmeet Dhillon, Trump's assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division at the U.S. Department of Justice, added.

title: Gmail change may flood your inbox with political email
summary: Gmail's Verified Sender Program launches September 8, 2026, giving U.S. political committees a more reliable path to your personal email inbox.
story: Google General Counsel Halimah Delaine Prado joins 'Fox & Friends' to detail how Google is fighting AI-powered phishing scams.

If your Gmail inbox already feels crowded, election season may add another layer of noise. Starting Sept. 8, 2026, Google's new Gmail Verified Sender Program will give qualifying U.S. political committees a more reliable path to personal Gmail accounts. That means qualifying political committees will have a new way to improve the reliability of their email delivery, provided they follow Google's security, authentication and spam requirements.

The program applies to eligible candidates, parties, PACs and other registered political committees that meet Google's requirements. Campaign Verify's eligibility criteria focus on registration and program requirements, regardless of party label.
The bigger issue for you is control. You can still unsubscribe, block a sender, report unwanted messages as spam or create your own Gmail filters.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
DO NOT CLICK FAKE 'ACCOUNT RECOVERY' AMAZON EMAIL
Google’s new Verified Sender Program could make it easier for qualifying political emails to reach your Gmail inbox starting September 8. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What is Gmail's Verified Sender Program?

The Gmail Verified Sender Program is scheduled to launch September 8 for eligible U.S. political committees. Campaign Verify says political organizations must verify their sending domains before they can participate. Eligible groups include candidates, parties, PACs and other political committees that qualify under the program. Google also requires participating senders to follow email security and compliance rules. One key requirement is a user-reported spam rate below 0.3% over a rolling 14-day average.

Getting verified alone does not guarantee that every campaign message will reach your inbox. Google says continued participation depends on senders following its requirements and maintaining positive recipient engagement. If a sender's average user-reported spam rate rises above 0.3% over a rolling 14-day period, the sender violates the program's policy and could be suspended or removed. Standard Gmail spam filtering would then apply.

So, this does not give campaigns unlimited access to your inbox. However, it changes how Gmail can treat eligible political email before you personally tell Gmail what you want. One more point: verification confirms the political committee's sending domain. It should not be read as Google vouching for every claim, fundraising pitch or link inside a message.
Why you may notice more political email

Here is the part that could get annoying. Gmail has long used automated systems to decide whether bulk email belongs in your inbox or spam folder. Under the new program, verified political senders that stay within Google's rules can receive more reliable delivery to personal Gmail accounts.

For someone who already receives fundraising appeals, petition requests or campaign updates, that could mean seeing more political messages in Gmail. Google tells CyberGuy the program grew out of an earlier pilot and says Gmail users will remain in control of what stays in their inboxes.

"Following our previous pilot, this program is designed to connect people with the emails they want to receive while keeping them fully in control of their inboxes. To participate, bulk senders must meet strict security and compliance requirements, ensuring that messages people receive are relevant, useful, and verified," a Google spokesperson told CyberGuy.

Google also points out that Gmail users can continue to mark a message as spam, block a specific sender and unsubscribe from unwanted mailing lists. The company says the new program does not turn off Gmail's broader security protections. Google says Gmail's filters continue to block more than 99.9% of spam, phishing and malware while using recipient feedback to help determine what people want to receive. Still, if more qualifying political messages reach you, some of the cleanup work may fall on you.
RUSSIAN HACKERS CAN STEAL EMAILS WITHOUT A CLICK
Gmail users can still unsubscribe, report unwanted messages as spam, block senders and create filters to reduce campaign email clutter. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What happens if you mark a political email as spam?

This is where your own Gmail choices become important. According to reporting on the new program, if you mark a participating sender's message as spam, Gmail can use that feedback for your account. Future messages from that sender can then be routed to spam based on your preference.

Google's standard Gmail tools also confirm that messages you report as spam move into the Spam folder. Over time, reporting unwanted email helps Gmail identify similar messages more effectively. In other words, do not assume you have to live with every campaign message that reaches you.
Tips to cut down political email in Gmail
You have several ways to take back your inbox. Start with the least aggressive option and move up if the messages keep coming.

On a computer, open the message and look next to the sender's name. If Gmail shows an Unsubscribe option, click it and confirm. Google says some unsubscribe requests can take a few days to fully stop the mail. Gmail may also send you to the sender's website when a one-click option is unavailable.

If you did not ask for the message or the sender keeps emailing you after you tried to leave the list, select the email and click Report spam. That moves the message into Spam and gives Gmail another signal about what you do not want.

For a sender you never want to hear from again, Gmail lets you block that address. Future messages from a blocked sender go to Spam. Keep in mind that campaigns may use more than one sending address or domain. Blocking one address may reduce the flow without stopping every related message.

If the same sender or phrase keeps showing up, create a filter on your computer. Open Gmail, click Show search options in the search box and enter the sender, domain or other criteria you want to target. Then click Create filter and choose what Gmail should do with matching messages. You can archive them, apply a label or delete them automatically. I would be careful with broad keywords such as "vote" or "election." Those words can appear in news alerts, community messages and emails you actually want. A specific sender or domain gives you more control.
FAR-LEFT POLITICIANS STILL USING ACTBLUE AS 88-YEAR-OLD DISPUTES DONATING NEARLY $150,000 TO FUNDRAISING GIANT
As election season heats up, political email could become more noticeable in your inbox, making your own spam controls more important. (Photo by Ute Grabowsky/Photothek via Getty Images)

Political campaigns and other organizations can obtain contact information from many sources, including public records and commercial data providers. Reducing the amount of personal information circulating online may help limit some unwanted outreach.

A personal data removal service can do much of the cleanup for you. They can send removal requests to data brokers on your behalf and continue following up as your information reappears. This can reduce your exposure across data broker and people-search sites. However, it cannot remove information from government websites, so it will not stop every political email or message.

The less personal information that data brokers have available to package and share, the fewer places marketers and other organizations may have to find your contact details. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com.

Political email can also give scammers an easy theme to copy. If a message pressures you to donate immediately, verify your identity or click a link before a deadline, avoid using the link in the email when anything feels off. Go directly to the campaign or organization's official website instead. CyberGuy has covered how scammers use fake political donation requests and how political messages can hide scam links.

One of the best ways to reduce future clutter is to stop handing out your main email address everywhere. An email alias gives you another address that forwards to your inbox. You can use a separate alias for donations, petitions, newsletters or other sign-ups. If that alias starts getting flooded, you can shut it down without changing your primary address. For recommendations on private and secure email providers that offer alias addresses, visit Cyberguy.com.
This Gmail change arrives at a time when many people already feel buried by junk email, spam texts, robocalls and political messages.

We covered exactly that in our free CyberGuy LIVE class, "Sick of Spam?" The live session has ended, but you can still get the replay and our spam-stopping checklist. I walk you through ways to reduce junk email, cut down robocalls, curb political texts and clean up unwanted messages. Get the free CyberGuy LIVE replay and checklist at Cyberguy.com/cyberguylive/classes/#past-classes. That is worth doing before September 8, especially if your inbox already feels like a dumping ground.
Kurt's key takeaways

Google is giving verified political committees a new path to more reliable email delivery, but campaigns still have to play by Gmail's rules. Users also retain the power to unsubscribe, block senders and hit the spam button. From a security standpoint, verifying political senders can help make impersonation harder. From an inbox standpoint, however, you may still end up doing more of the sorting yourself if campaign volume picks up. My advice is simple: use Gmail's controls aggressively when a message keeps showing up after you have had enough. Unsubscribe from legitimate lists. Report suspicious or unwanted messages as spam. Create targeted filters for repeat senders. Then think about using an alias for future political sign-ups so your primary email stays cleaner. Google's 0.3% spam threshold also gives campaigns a strong incentive to avoid irritating recipients. The real test will come after September 8, when political email volume increases and Gmail users start voting with the Report spam button.

title: Pilotless cargo aircraft could change how packages move
summary: Elroy Air's Chaparral can carry over 500 pounds and fly 450 miles without a runway, and the FAA just tested it under a new federal program.
story: A medical drone takes off during testing as part of a program aimed at speeding up the delivery of critical healthcare supplies. The effort is focused on transporting lab samples, blood and donor matching materials between smaller communities and larger hospital hubs, where timing can impact diagnoses and treatment. Developers say faster, on-demand flights could help reduce delays for rural patients, who often face longer travel times for care, with future plans to expand the technology to carry transplant-related materials.

A broken pump on an offshore platform, or medical supplies needed after a hurricane can be tough to move quickly. The FAA just tested one possible solution: a hybrid-electric cargo aircraft that can take off vertically and fly without a crew onboard.

The FAA announced that Elroy Air and the Louisiana Department of Transportation and Development conducted a cargo demonstration at Houma-Terrebonne Airport in Louisiana. The agency says it was the first remotely piloted aircraft test flight under its eVTOL (electric vertical takeoff and landing) Integration Pilot Program, known as eIPP.

That may sound like a specialized aviation test, but the bigger story is what aircraft like this could eventually do. Elroy Air's Chaparral can carry more than 500 pounds, putting it in a very different league from the small delivery drones you may picture hovering over a driveway.

So, could pilotless aircraft like this eventually change how everything from emergency supplies to everyday goods moves across the country? Here's what the FAA is testing and why it could be a big deal.
MISSOURI TESTS MEDICAL DRONES TO SPEED UP RURAL HEALTH CARE
The Chaparral can take off and land vertically, allowing it to operate in places without a traditional runway. (Elroy Air)

Why this pilotless cargo aircraft test stands out

The FAA created eIPP to help the government learn how next-generation aircraft can operate safely in U.S. airspace. In March, the Department of Transportation selected eight projects across 26 states. Louisiana is one of the participants, and more test flights are planned through the rest of 2026. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the Louisiana demonstration provides data that can help "turn these concepts from trial to deployment."

That line gets to the heart of this test. Chaparral has flown before. In December 2025, Elroy Air completed its first point-to-point cargo delivery with the aircraft. During that demonstration, Chaparral autonomously carried 213 pounds over a 2.6-mile flight. What changed here is the regulatory setting. The FAA now gets to study these flights as part of a federal program focused on bringing advanced aircraft into the national airspace.
How Elroy Air's Chaparral works

Chaparral looks more like a small cargo aircraft than the drone that might bring dinner to your house. It uses electric propulsion for vertical takeoff and landing. Then it transitions to wingborne flight for the longer part of the trip. A hybrid-electric powertrain gives the aircraft longer-range capability without requiring charging infrastructure at every stop. Elroy Air's current Chaparral specifications list a maximum range of 450 miles and a payload of more than 500 pounds.

The cargo system is unusual, too. Elroy designed modular pods that workers can load before the aircraft arrives. Chaparral can pick up a pod, fly it to another location and leave it there. That could reduce the amount of ground equipment needed at remote sites. Because it can take off vertically, Chaparral can serve locations that lack a traditional runway.
Pilotless still involves human oversight

There is an important detail behind the word "pilotless." The FAA described the Louisiana demonstration as remotely piloted. Elroy Air later said Chaparral completed a week-long series of flights autonomously with no pilot onboard while operating under Air Traffic Control oversight.

That means humans still play a role in overseeing these operations even when the aircraft handles the flight autonomously. As testing continues, regulators will have to determine how much human supervision is required and how the aircraft should respond to communication failures, changing weather or other unexpected problems.
DOORDASH GETS FAA APPROVAL FOR ITS OWN DELIVERY DRONES
Elroy Air designed the Chaparral to carry heavy cargo between locations, including remote worksites and areas that are difficult to reach by road. (Elroy Air)
Where Chaparral could be useful first

You probably will not see a Chaparral dropping an Amazon box onto your front lawn anytime soon. The aircraft targets what the logistics industry calls the middle mile. That means moving cargo between larger points in a delivery network rather than carrying one small order to your doorstep.

Elroy Air has pointed to offshore energy operations and industrial supply chains as potential uses. The company also sees an opportunity in disaster response, where damaged roads can make moving supplies far more difficult. For example, Chaparral could carry replacement equipment to an offshore facility without sending a crewed helicopter. After a major storm, aircraft like it could eventually help move heavier supplies into areas that ground vehicles struggle to reach.
Elroy Air said when it joined eIPP earlier this year that the program could include cargo operations across the Gulf Coast, including energy industry locations in Louisiana, Texas and Mississippi.
How this fits into the delivery boom

Delivery drones are starting to show up in more places, but most of them are still carrying pretty small loads. Amazon plans to expand Prime Air drone delivery to nearly 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of 2026. Those drones are built for lightweight packages delivered directly to customers. We recently took a closer look at Amazon's huge drone delivery expansion and what it could mean if you live in one of the communities getting the service.
Meanwhile, other companies are working on the last part of the trip. Robot.com's R-dog uses wheeled legs to get over obstacles such as stairs and curbs while carrying deliveries.

Chaparral takes on a much bigger job. Instead of carrying one sandwich or a small box, it is built to move substantial cargo between locations. That could make heavy-duty delivery one of the first places where this kind of aircraft proves especially useful.
What happens next for the FAA program

The Louisiana flight represents one step in a much broader federal test program. The FAA says it will study these demonstrations, identify problems and refine procedures for advanced air mobility. Louisiana and the other eIPP participants plan additional flights through the rest of the year.

Watch how much human supervision the FAA requires as the technology develops. Regulators will also have to decide where these aircraft can operate routinely. Another major test will come when something goes wrong. Communication can fail. Weather can change. The aircraft will need dependable ways to respond safely when either happens. Those answers will tell us much more about how close pilotless cargo aircraft are to regular commercial use.
100 KODIAK DRIVERLESS TRUCKS ARE HEADED FOR PUBLIC ROADS
Elroy Air’s Chaparral hybrid-electric cargo aircraft takes flight as the FAA tests how remotely piloted aircraft could fit into U.S. airspace. (Elroy Air)
What this means to you

The biggest change could happen behind the scenes before you ever see one of these aircraft overhead. If heavy cargo can move faster between remote locations, companies could shorten some supply routes. Communities that are expensive or difficult to reach could gain another delivery option.
Emergency response could benefit as well. An aircraft that takes off without a runway could potentially keep supplies moving when damaged infrastructure slows trucks or traditional aircraft.
However, communities will want answers about noise and flight paths. Safety questions will be even bigger as these aircraft begin sharing more airspace with conventional aviation.
For you, the FAA's work now could eventually influence which autonomous delivery services reach your area and what safeguards come with them.
Kurt's key takeaways

What gets my attention here is how much work this aircraft could actually take on. We have watched small delivery drones inch closer to everyday use for years, but Chaparral is built for a much bigger job. It can move hundreds of pounds over real distances without needing a runway at every stop. I also like that the FAA is testing this in a real-world program instead of rushing it into wider use. Regulators need to see how these aircraft handle shared airspace, changing conditions and unexpected problems. The bar should stay high when you are talking about hundreds of pounds flying overhead. For now, I would keep an eye on remote worksites, disaster response and other places where moving cargo is difficult or slow. If these aircraft prove they can do that safely and reliably, they could end up changing a much bigger part of the delivery network.

title: Autonomous excavators are digging with empty cabs
summary: Bedrock Robotics says its autonomous excavators are doing paid earthwork on active job sites in Texas and Nevada with no operator in the cab.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

If you have ever driven past a construction site and watched an excavator moving huge piles of dirt, you probably figured there was an experienced operator sitting in the cab. On some job sites in Texas and Nevada, there is nobody in that seat.

San Francisco-based Bedrock Robotics has autonomous excavators doing real commercial earthwork with no operator onboard. The company says the deployments follow a year of testing on active job sites with human supervision.

Seeing AI take over software tasks is one thing. Watching it control a massive excavator on a live construction site feels very different. Bedrock says this could help contractors deal with worker shortages and keep projects moving more efficiently. Here's how the technology works and what could come next.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
100 KODIAK DRIVERLESS TRUCKS ARE HEADED FOR PUBLIC ROADS
Bedrock’s sensor and computing system gives an excavator the technology it needs to operate autonomously. (Bedrock Robotics)
Bedrock's autonomous excavators are working on real projects

Bedrock says its operator-free excavators are now active on major infrastructure projects. One machine is working on a Nevada water treatment facility with Sundt Construction. In Texas, Bedrock is working with Champion Site Prep on a multimillion-cubic-yard earthwork project.
The company also has a 1.2 million-cubic-yard civil sitework project with Zachry Construction Corporation. The current work centers on rough early earthmoving and foundation prep.

The company is concentrating on clearing earth, cut-and-fill operations and rough cuts before moving into more detailed work. That makes sense because earthwork comes early in a project. If crews fall behind there, everything that follows can feel the delay.
Bedrock says productivity is approaching human levels
Bedrock measures excavator productivity by the cubic yards of earth moved during a shift, a company spokesperson tells CyberGuy.

How much earth a machine should move depends on the project, soil conditions and the rest of the equipment involved. Still, the spokesperson says, "As of our deployments in August 2026, two years after the company was founded, we are already near human-level productivity."
How the Bedrock Operator makes an excavator autonomous

Bedrock calls its system the Bedrock Operator. The company designed it as a retrofit for existing heavy equipment. Bedrock says crews can install its sensor and computing package in a day without permanent changes to the machine. Once a site manager sets the initial plan, the software takes over the digging work. Bedrock says its machine-learning system can understand the surrounding area and plan movement. It can then carry out complex tasks.

The company says it trained the system on tens of thousands of hours of field work. However, there is an important detail about the current rollout. Bedrock is deploying new excavators that it outfitted and tested at its own facilities. When we asked when the system would begin operating on contractors' existing equipment, a Bedrock spokesperson said the company has no update to share yet but hopes to have more soon. So the retrofit model remains central to Bedrock's plan. The live operator-free deployments are still in an earlier phase.
An empty cab still comes with human oversight

Seeing a huge excavator move with nobody inside will probably make some people nervous. Bedrock knows safety will help determine how far this technology goes and says it comes first as the company expands deployment. The machines monitor their own progress while they work. If a machine gets stuck or cannot continue, the system can call for help.

When we asked how often a person needs to step in, a Bedrock spokesperson told CyberGuy, "It's relatively rare." If a machine encounters something unusual or gets stuck, someone monitoring the fleet can briefly intervene until the autonomous system is ready to take back over.

Bedrock also keeps a person in the loop. That gives the system a path to human support without requiring someone to sit in the cab all day. On active sites, that becomes especially important. People walk through work zones. Water trucks and other heavy equipment move nearby.

Bedrock says the safety response happens automatically. "If a person or unauthorized object gets too close to a Bedrock-equipped machine, the machine will automatically stop," the spokesperson said. The excavator stays stopped until the person or object has moved to a safe distance, with no manual intervention required.
HUMANLESS BIG RIG COMPLETES FIRST US FREIGHT RUN
The empty cab shows how Bedrock’s system can handle digging work without an operator sitting inside. (Bedrock Robotics)
Why Bedrock started with one of the hardest machines
Bedrock picked excavators for a reason. The company says excavators can account for about 25% of a contractor's fleet. They also take years to master.

Bedrock estimates that an operator may need five years or more to fully develop the skill. That creates a difficult staffing problem. Contractors need experienced people, yet many projects involve long stretches of repetitive earthmoving.
Bedrock wants autonomous equipment to handle more of that repeatable production work. Skilled operators could then focus on detailed jobs or supervise a larger operation.
We have seen autonomous excavators before. CyberGuy previously covered HEAP, a 12-ton robotic excavator that built a massive stone wall on its own.
What makes Bedrock different is where the technology is headed now. These excavators are doing commercial work on active job sites as part of real infrastructure projects.
Construction faces a growing worker shortage

The timing helps explain why investors are pouring money into this technology. Bedrock has raised more than $350 million. Its founding team includes former Waymo engineers who spent years working on autonomous vehicles.

Meanwhile, construction companies are struggling to find enough skilled workers. Bedrock cites industry estimates showing that roughly one in five construction workers is over age 55. Another estimate says more than 40% of the construction workforce could retire within the next five years.

The company also points to research showing that 92% of firms with open craft positions have difficulty filling at least some of those jobs. Those departures could hit contractors while demand remains high across many types of building projects.
Costs add another pressure point. Bedrock cites a McKinsey analysis that found large construction projects typically took 20% longer than scheduled and ran up to 80% over budget.

Then there is safety. Construction accounts for a disproportionate share of workplace deaths compared with its share of the overall workforce. Automation could help reduce exposure to dangerous tasks. However, companies will still need to prove that autonomous machines can work safely around people over long periods.

Bedrock also takes a firm position on what this technology means for equipment operators. "We do not expect operators to be replaced at all," a Bedrock spokesperson tells CyberGuy. In the near term, the company sees Bedrock-equipped machines working alongside existing crews because contractors do not have enough skilled operators to tackle every project. Longer term, Bedrock expects some experienced operators to move into supervisory positions overseeing autonomous equipment. The company compares that future role to becoming a "foreman for machines." At the same time, Bedrock says people who want to continue operating equipment themselves should still have a place in construction for years to come.
Bedrock wants machines to work together next

The long-term idea goes far beyond one excavator digging by itself. Bedrock wants multiple machines to coordinate across a job site. Bedrock co-founder Kevin Peterson described a future where an excavator could work alongside a bulldozer, truck and grader.

Instead of each machine operating as a separate tool, software could help coordinate the larger job. That could change project scheduling in a big way. A site manager might eventually assign the goal while a connected fleet determines how to move the work forward.
Bedrock says this coordinated model remains on its roadmap. For now, the company is scaling excavator deployments and expanding the types of tasks its system can perform.
Bedrock keeps a person in the loop to monitor operations and step in when the autonomous system needs help. (Bedrock Robotics)
What this means to you

Here's why this could affect you. Construction delays can hold up new housing, road projects and water infrastructure. If autonomous equipment can keep earthwork moving when contractors cannot find enough experienced operators, some projects could move faster and stay closer to schedule.

Bedrock says it sees autonomous machines working alongside people rather than eliminating operator jobs. In the near term, that could give existing crews more help with repetitive earthwork. Over time, some experienced operators could end up supervising groups of autonomous machines while others continue working directly in the cab.
Permits and material shortages can still slow a project down. Skilled workers also remain essential for planning, detailed work and handling situations the technology cannot manage on its own.

I'll be watching whether that near-human productivity holds up as these machines move onto more job sites. Bedrock says human intervention is relatively rare today, but I also want to see how that changes when one person is monitoring a larger fleet.

Safety will be the other big test. I want to see what happens when something unexpected enters the work zone. The more autonomous equipment we put around people, the more important that real-world track record becomes.
Kurt's key takeaways

What catches my attention here is that Bedrock has moved beyond showing what an autonomous excavator might be able to do someday. These machines are already doing paid work on active construction sites with nobody sitting in the cab. Bedrock now tells us the machines are nearing human-level productivity and that human intervention is "relatively rare." Those are encouraging signs, but I want to see how those claims hold up across more projects and over longer periods. I also like hearing Bedrock say directly that it does not expect operators to disappear. If autonomy helps contractors handle more work while experienced people take on tougher jobs or supervise the machines, there could be a real upside for both crews and the projects they build. The real test will come as Bedrock puts more of these machines to work. If they stay safe and productive around real crews, those empty cabs may become a much more familiar sight.

title: Should you use a separate computer for online banking?
summary: A dedicated banking computer isolates your financial accounts from malware and phishing, but passwords, SIM swapping and outdated software remain risks.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

When so much of your financial life lives online, protecting the device you use to access your money deserves some extra thought. Nancy from Baton Rouge, Louisiana, recently wrote to us asking whether keeping banking and investments on an entirely separate computer could provide another layer of protection.

"I've had several clients tell me they have bought a computer that is only used for online banking, financial institutions and anything to do with their investment accounts. Is this a good strategy for protecting some of your assets? What are the upsides and what are the downsides?"

Nancy, yes. Using a separate computer only for banking, investments and other financial accounts can add a meaningful layer of security. I especially like this approach for someone with substantial savings or retirement assets. It can also make sense if you simply want to keep your financial life separated from everything else you do online.
However, buying another computer will not make your accounts untouchable. How you set it up and how you use it are what make the strategy worthwhile.

CYBERCRIME LOSSES NEAR $21B: 5 WAYS TO PROTECT YOUR MONEY
A dedicated computer used only for banking and investments can reduce exposure to many everyday online threats. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why a separate computer for online banking can help

Think about what happens on the computer you use every day. You open email, click links and shop online. Maybe you also use social media, download documents or install browser extensions. All of that creates opportunities for malware, phishing attempts or malicious software to reach your device. A dedicated financial computer removes much of that exposure.

On this computer, you would skip email and casual web browsing. Online shopping would happen on another device. Ideally, you would install very little software beyond what the computer needs for security and accessing your financial accounts. That gives attackers fewer opportunities to reach the device you use to manage your money. Our guide to safely viewing your bank and retirement accounts online also explains why protecting the device you use is an important part of financial security.
The biggest benefits of a banking-only computer
The biggest advantage is isolation. If malware gets onto the laptop you use for email or everyday browsing, your dedicated financial computer remains separate.
There are several other benefits worth considering:

Less exposure to malware and phishing: You are not opening random links or attachments on the same computer that accesses your financial accounts.A cleaner computer: You can limit installed software and avoid unnecessary browser extensions that could introduce security risks.More control over where you sign in: You can bookmark your legitimate bank and investment websites and use those bookmarks every time.Everyday mistakes stay somewhere else: A malicious download or dangerous website on your regular computer is less likely to affect the device you use for financial accounts.
Less exposure to malware and phishing: You are not opening random links or attachments on the same computer that accesses your financial accounts.
A cleaner computer: You can limit installed software and avoid unnecessary browser extensions that could introduce security risks.
More control over where you sign in: You can bookmark your legitimate bank and investment websites and use those bookmarks every time.
Everyday mistakes stay somewhere else: A malicious download or dangerous website on your regular computer is less likely to affect the device you use for financial accounts.
For people who do not need to check investments constantly, that separation can be especially useful.
FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK
Keeping your financial computer updated and limiting what you do on it can help strengthen its security. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
A dedicated banking computer still has weaknesses
This is where you need to be careful. A banking-only computer can reduce certain risks, but it cannot protect you from every way criminals may try to reach your money.

If you reuse a password that later appears in a data breach, having a separate computer will not solve the problem. Every financial account should have its own strong password. A password manager can help create and securely store unique passwords for you.

Many financial institutions still use text messages to send security codes. Criminals may try to hijack a victim's phone number through SIM swapping or an unauthorized number transfer. If that happens, they could potentially receive verification messages without ever touching your banking computer. Our guide on how to avoid a malicious SIM swapping scam explains how protections such as a carrier PIN or number-transfer lock can help reduce that risk.

Suppose you receive an alarming text on your phone claiming someone transferred thousands of dollars from your account. You walk over to the dedicated computer and type the website address included in that message. If the address leads to a phishing site, the separate computer cannot protect you from entering your login information there. That is why I recommend bookmarking your financial institutions' legitimate websites and using those bookmarks rather than following addresses sent through unexpected emails or texts.

A computer that spends most of its life sitting unused can create another problem. It still needs security updates. Operating system and browser updates regularly fix vulnerabilities that criminals may try to exploit. Keep automatic updates enabled and restart the computer when necessary. If you have not used the financial computer in several weeks, let it finish installing updates before signing into your accounts.
Strong passwords, secure authentication and account alerts still matter, even when you use a separate computer for your finances. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Tips for setting up a separate computer for online banking
If you decide to take this approach, keep the computer's purpose very narrow. The less you do on it, the more useful the separation becomes.
Keep Windows, macOS or ChromeOS updated automatically. Your browser should stay updated too. Do not keep postponing restarts when an important security update requires one.

Reserve it for your bank, brokerage accounts, retirement plans, credit cards and other important financial services. Avoid email and social media. Do your online shopping and everyday browsing on another device.

I would also keep strong antivirus software running on the dedicated computer. Look for protection that can detect malware, phishing attempts and other online threats in real time. Even on a computer with limited use, antivirus software adds another layer of protection in case a malicious website or other threat reaches the device. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Go directly to your financial institution's legitimate website and save it as a bookmark. Then use that bookmark whenever you need to sign in. Be especially careful with financial links that arrive through text messages or emails, even when they appear urgent.

Never reuse your banking password somewhere else. If another website suffers a data breach, criminals may try stolen usernames and passwords on financial accounts. A password manager can create strong, unique passwords and remember them for you.

Enable multi-factor authentication on every financial account that supports it. If your institution offers a passkey or physical security key, consider using it. An authenticator app may also provide stronger protection than receiving a verification code by text. For more on the differences, see our guide to whether bank text codes are enough to protect you.

Do not wait until your monthly statement arrives to discover suspicious activity. Set alerts for logins, withdrawals, transfers, new payees and password changes whenever your financial institution offers them. These notifications can give you an early warning when something happens that you did not authorize.
Is a separate banking computer necessary for everyone?

No. You can safely manage financial accounts from a well-maintained everyday computer if you follow strong security practices. Keep the computer updated. Protect each financial account with a unique password and use strong authentication whenever possible.

For many people, those protections combined with careful online behavior will provide strong security. However, I look at the equation a little differently for someone managing significant retirement savings or investment assets. The cost of a basic computer may be relatively small compared with the amount of money you are trying to protect. You also do not need an expensive machine for banking and investment websites.

If you decide the extra separation makes sense for you, take a look at my best laptops for 2026 and best desktop computers for 2026 at Cyberguy.com to compare current options. A dedicated machine can create a cleaner and more controlled environment for accessing your financial accounts. Just remember that the separation only works if you maintain it. Once the "banking computer" becomes the computer you also use for email, social media or general web browsing, much of that security advantage disappears.
Kurt's key takeaways

Nancy's question gets at something I wish more people thought about before a scam or account takeover happens. A separate computer for online banking can be a smart additional barrier, particularly when you are protecting significant savings or retirement assets. Keeping email, downloads and everyday web activity away from that machine reduces the opportunities criminals have to reach it. Still, I would never rely on the computer alone. Your passwords matter. Your phone number needs protection. Strong authentication can help stop someone who gets hold of a password, while account alerts can warn you when something suspicious happens. So, if buying a dedicated computer gives you greater control over how you access your money, I think it is a sensible strategy. Treat it as another layer in a larger financial security plan rather than a replacement for the protections you already need. title: AI robot pet could know your family too well
summary: The OlloNi SS1 AI robot pet uses a 4K camera and facial recognition to learn your family, but its removable Red Heart memory module raises questions.
story: The 'Cyber Guy' Kurt Knutsson cautions parents about AI-powered chatbot teddy bears, highlighting privacy risks as toys might collect children's personal details.

We've covered home robots that can fold laundry and others designed to become AI companions. Now there's one that wants to remember your family. The OlloNi SS1 is an AI robot pet that can recognize family members and pets as it moves around your home. OlloBot says it can learn your routines, respond to emotional cues and save memorable family moments along the way.

Here's where it gets really interesting. OlloNi has a removable "Red Heart" memory module designed to carry those memories into a future OlloBot. So, when the robot gets replaced, years of personalization could move right along with you.

I can see the appeal of that. I also think it's important to ask yourself this: How much of your family's life are you comfortable letting a robot remember? Here's how OlloNi works, what it can remember and the privacy questions to consider before deciding whether you'd want one in your home.
WOULD YOU PAY $8,000 FOR A ROBOT TO FOLD LAUNDRY?
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. The OlloNi SS1 artificial intelligence robot pet can recognize family members and pets, learn household routines and capture memorable moments with a 4K camera. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What is the OlloNi SS1 AI robot pet?

The OlloNi SS1 is OlloBot's newest AI companion robot pet, developed by Hong Kong-based Ollobot Robotics Limited. Unlike a robot built mainly for chores, the SS1 is designed to interact with the people and pets living around it.

Two circular eye screens display expressions while a separate main screen handles information and direct interaction. The setup gives OlloNi a face that can react visually without relying on spoken responses every time.

A 4K camera with motion tracking helps the robot recognize individual family members and household pets. OlloBot says the SS1 gradually learns routines and preferences as it spends more time with a household. It also adapts to different communication patterns.
That puts OlloNi in a different category from a robot vacuum or a machine built mainly to handle physical work. The goal here is to make the robot feel increasingly familiar.
OlloNi wants to understand how you are feeling

OlloBot is also giving the SS1 what it describes as proactive emotional interaction. The company says the robot uses several types of information to interpret what is happening around it. That includes someone's tone of voice and facial expression. It can also learn behavioral patterns over time.
For example, OlloBot says the robot may notice when someone appears to be feeling low. Instead of waiting for that person to issue a command, OlloNi could approach and initiate an interaction.

We recently covered Familiar, another emotionally aware AI robot pet. That robot is also designed to learn routines and react to the people around it. OlloNi takes the idea in another direction by connecting that personalization to a memory system that can survive beyond the original robot.
A 4K camera can capture family moments for you

One feature I can see families using is OlloNi's 4K camera. With permission turned on, OlloBot says the SS1 can recognize moments such as laughter or celebrations and capture them automatically. Its AI-assisted Vlog feature can then edit the footage and add music to create home videos.
I like the idea behind this. When something memorable happens, someone usually reaches for a phone. That often means the person recording ends up watching part of the moment through a screen.
OlloNi could change that. Because the robot is already moving around the home, it could capture moments while everyone else stays in them.
But this is also where I would start thinking seriously about privacy. You are allowing a connected 4K camera to move around your home and decide which moments may be worth saving.
That is a lot of access to give any device, no matter how cute the robot looks.
OlloNi can become a moving window into your home

OlloNi also supports remote viewing and two-way voice and video calls. Unlike a camera sitting on a shelf, the robot can move around the home and follow activity. OlloBot says this could make remote check-ins feel more active for family members who live apart.

The idea could appeal to someone who wants to stay connected with an older relative or other family members from a distance. OlloBot's website also says its app can let you see and interact with OlloNi while you are away. The app is designed to show daily moments and memories the robot has captured.

However, remote access raises the stakes for security. A camera that can move around your house deserves strong account protection. Owners should know exactly who can connect to it and what happens if an account gets compromised.
The Red Heart lets OlloNi's memories live on

This may be the most unusual part of the SS1. OlloBot calls it the Red Heart. The detachable module has 16GB of RAM and 64GB of local storage. OlloBot says the module carries the robot's long-term memories and personalized information.

Now, imagine replacing the robot several years from now. Instead of starting over, OlloBot says you could move the Red Heart into a future-generation OlloBot. Family memories and personalized information could then follow you to the next device. That is a clever idea. Most gadgets become disposable once their hardware gets old. OlloBot wants the relationship you developed with this one to survive the upgrade.

At the same time, think about how personal that little module could become. Years of family life could potentially be tied to it. That makes the Red Heart something I would want protected every bit as carefully as the robot itself.
OlloNi SS1 privacy deserves a closer look

This is where I would slow down and read the fine print. OlloBot says the SS1 uses local encrypted processing and includes a physical camera cover. The company also says facial recognition and automatic family moment capture work with your permission.

Those are good things to see. Still, a robot that can move around your home, recognize faces and build memories over time deserves more than a quick glance at the privacy settings. OlloBot's current privacy policy was last updated July 6, 2026. It covers the company's store and broader services, including device and usage information collected when people interact with those services. The policy also says some information may be handled by outside vendors that provide services such as IT management, data analytics or cloud storage.

What I want to see next is something much more specific to the SS1 itself. If this robot can recognize your family and save moments inside your home, you should know exactly where that information goes. OlloBot should explain what stays on the Red Heart, what leaves the robot and how long anything gets stored.

I would also want a clear answer about deletion. If OlloNi spends years learning your routines and how your family interacts, you should be able to see what it knows and permanently erase that information when you want it gone.
AI WEARABLE WATCHES YOU TO PREDICT WHAT YOU NEED
OlloBot’s OlloNi SS1 uses a removable "Red Heart" memory module designed to transfer years of personalized memories to future robots. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
OlloBot's child privacy language needs clarification
There is another privacy point worth watching. OlloBot's Aug. 28 announcement lists children separated from their parents by distance among the potential users for the SS1.

Meanwhile, OlloBot's current privacy policy says its "services are not intended to be used by children." It also says the company does not knowingly collect personal information from children under the age of majority in the user's jurisdiction. That does not automatically mean there is a conflict.

The current policy appears geared largely toward OlloBot's store and broader services rather than offering a detailed privacy framework specifically for the SS1. Still, OlloBot should clarify how those terms apply when a product is designed to interact with families and potentially children inside the home. Parents should not have to guess.
What happens if someone gets your Red Heart?

This is one of the first questions I would ask about the Red Heart: What happens if you lose it? If your family has used OlloNi for years, that little removable module could contain a very personal history of life inside your home.

OlloBot says the SS1 uses local encrypted processing, which is encouraging. What I want to know is what happens when the Red Heart comes out of the robot. If someone finds or steals it, does the information remain encrypted and inaccessible? I would also want a way to remotely erase the module if it disappears.

The whole appeal of the Red Heart is that families could keep it for years and move their memories into a future OlloBot. If OlloBot wants us to hold onto something that personal for that long, I want to know exactly how it will keep those memories protected.
OlloNi also keeps track of its surroundings

OlloNi goes beyond watching the people around it. The robot also pays attention to what is happening inside the home. OlloBot says the SS1 includes temperature and humidity sensors along with ambient light and spatial sensors. That gives the robot more context about its surroundings. The company says those sensors can help with reminders and brief activity records tied to relevant interactions rather than continuous recording.
The OlloNi SS1 crowdfunding launch has been postponed
If all of this has you wondering what the robot costs, there is a catch. You cannot back the planned SS1 crowdfunding campaign right now.
OlloBot previously said it would launch the OlloNi SS1 globally on Kickstarter in August 2026. In July, the company narrowed that window to late August. Then the plan changed.

On Aug. 28, OlloBot announced that it had postponed the crowdfunding launch. The company pointed to recent changes in the U.S. regulatory and market access environment for robotic devices made abroad. OlloBot says it wants a clear path to market and fulfillment before moving forward.

For now, the company has not announced a new crowdfunding date. OlloBot says it will share an updated timeline through its official channels once one is confirmed. So, consider the SS1 a robot to watch rather than one you can order today.
What this means to you

OlloNi SS1 shows how quickly the idea of a home robot is changing. We have spent years watching robots get better at physical work. Now companies want these machines to learn about the people living around them. That changes what you need to consider before bringing one home.
With a robot like OlloNi, start by looking beyond the cute eyes. Find out what its camera records and who can access those recordings. Next, understand the memory system.

You should know what stays locally on the robot and what gets transmitted elsewhere. Also check whether you can permanently delete information when you want it gone. Remote access deserves attention too. Look for strong account security and controls that let you shut off features you do not use.

Finally, think about the lifespan of your data. The entire point of the Red Heart is to keep personalized information after you replace the robot. That makes long-term software support especially important.

We recently saw why connected robots deserve scrutiny when a security report raised concerns about a Yarbo robot mower. The issues involved remote access, cameras and home-network exposure. Yarbo later acknowledged the core technical findings and began rolling out fixes.

OlloBot has already said it uses local encrypted processing and includes a physical camera cover. Now I want to see the deeper security details behind those promises. We reached out to OlloBot with questions about data storage, remote access and Red Heart security but did not hear back before our deadline.
MAJORITY OF YOUNG ADULTS SAY THEY ARE 'MORE CONCERNED THAN EXCITED' ABOUT AI: PEW RESEARCH
The OlloNi SS1 can interpret facial expressions, tone of voice and behavioral patterns as it learns how people interact inside the home. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Kurt's key takeaways

OlloNi SS1 caught my attention because OlloBot wants this robot to become more personal the longer it lives with you. The Red Heart is the feature I keep coming back to. Instead of losing years of personalization when the hardware gets old, your family's memories could move into the next robot. I can see why that might feel special.

I can also see why some people will want the exact opposite. A robot that recognizes your family and captures private moments can learn a lot about what happens behind your front door. When those memories are designed to last for years, privacy becomes part of the buying decision from day one.

OlloBot's physical camera cover and local encrypted processing are good places to start. Before anyone hands over money, though, I want clearer answers about recordings and remote access. The company also needs to explain exactly what happens to information stored in the Red Heart. That does not make OlloNi a robot to fear. It makes it a robot that asks for a lot of trust.

Would you want an AI pet remembering years of your family's life and carrying those memories into its next robot body, or would that feel like giving a machine too much access to your home? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com
